title: Basic genetic mechanisms – DNA replication, transcription, translation
blurb: How genetic information flows from DNA to protein.
h1: Basic genetic mechanisms – DNA replication, transcription, translation
lede: How genetic information flows from DNA to protein. Replication has three phases: initiation (origins, helicase, topoisomerase, SSB proteins), elongation (primase, RNA primer, DNA polymerase, leading vs lagging strand, Okazaki fragments) and termination (telomeres, telomerase). Transcription by RNA polymerase is followed by post-transcriptional modification (pre-mRNA → mRNA, splicing out introns). Translation on the ribosome uses the genetic code (codons, anticodons, start AUG, stops UAA/UAG/UGA). The lecture ends with post-translational modifications (phosphorylation is the most common).

questions.q: Which enzyme synthesises the RNA primer during DNA replication?
questions.e: Primase, a specialised RNA polymerase, makes the RNA primer. (Slides: p. 7)
The lagging strand is made discontinuously, away from the fork. (Slides: p. 8)

questions.q: Which enzyme relaxes supercoiled DNA during replication?
questions.e: Topoisomerase relaxes supercoiling; helicase separates strands. (Slides: p. 6)

questions.q: DNA polymerase synthesises new DNA in which direction?
questions.e: Only 5′→3′, which is why the lagging strand is discontinuous. (Slides: p. 8)
In the germ line, telomerase extends telomere repeats. (Slides: p. 9)

questions.q: The DNA template strand reads TAC. The mRNA will be:
Which statement about introns is correct?
questions.answer: They are removed from pre-mRNA by splicing
questions.e: Introns are non-coding and spliced out. (Slides: p. 20)
AUG is the start codon. (Slides: p. 30)

questions.q: Which is NOT a stop codon?
questions.e: Stops are UAA, UAG and UGA; AUG is start. (Slides: p. 32)

questions.answer: several codons can code for the same amino acid
questions.e: Degeneracy softens the effect of mutations. (Slides: p. 25)

questions.q: Which enzyme attaches amino acids to tRNA?
questions.e: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase uses ATP to load tRNAs. (Slides: p. 29)

questions.q: The most common post-translational modification is:
questions.e: Phosphorylation regulates enzyme activity and is the most common PTM. (Slides: p. 33)

items.n: Which enzyme carries out DNA replication?
items.a: DNA polymerase.

items.n: To which end does DNA polymerase add nucleotides?
items.a: The 3′ end of an existing strand.

items.n: What is DNA polymerase's error rate?
items.a: Less than 1 mistake per 10⁷ nucleotides (some polymerases also proofread).
Initiation, elongation, termination.
At origins of replication, recognised by initiator proteins (pre-replication complex).
Unwinds and separates the two DNA strands at the replication fork.
Relaxes supercoiled DNA ahead of helicase.
Bind single-stranded DNA and prevent re-annealing.
DNA polymerase cannot initiate a new strand; it only extends an existing 3′ end.

items.n: Which enzyme makes the RNA primer?
items.a: Primase (a specialised RNA polymerase).

items.n: In which direction is DNA synthesised?
items.a: Only 5′ → 3′.
Leading: continuous, toward the fork, one primer. Lagging: discontinuous, away from the fork, Okazaki fragments, many primers.
Short DNA pieces of the lagging strand, each starting with its own RNA primer.

items.n: What are replication forks and bubbles?
items.a: Forks are Y-shaped unwound regions; two forks moving in opposite directions from an origin form a bubble.
Repetitive DNA at chromosome ends that prevents gene loss caused by end shortening.

items.n: What does telomerase do, and where?
items.a: Extends telomere repeats, in the germ cell line.

items.n: When was the Nobel Prize for telomeres and telomerase awarded?

items.a: RNA polymerase.

items.n: Where does RNA polymerase bind to start transcription?
items.a: The promoter, together with general transcription factors.
GUA-AGC.
The primary transcript, containing exons and introns, before processing.
Exons are coding sequences; introns are non-coding and removed.
Removal of introns from pre-mRNA and joining of exons into one continuous molecule.
A triplet of mRNA bases encoding a particular amino acid.

items.n: How many entries does the genetic code table have?

items.a: Degenerate, non-overlapping (read 5′→3′), universal.

items.n: Why does a degenerate code help?
items.a: It softens the effect of mutations.

items.n: Which ribosomal subunit binds the mRNA first?
items.a: The small subunit, at the 5′ end.
